title: A java.time front for a legacy scheduler

blocks.text: The page's rule is to **convert at the boundary**: `java.time` inside, legacy types only where an old API demands them. An old job scheduler takes and returns `java.util.Date`:
Write `SchedulerAdapter`, which wraps a `LegacyScheduler` so that the rest of the code only sees `java.time`:

items: `schedule(String job, ZonedDateTime when)` schedules the job at that moment, to the millisecond, whatever zone `when` is written in. The legacy scheduler **keeps** the `Date` it receives, so every call must hand it a `Date` **of its own**.
`nextRun(String job, ZoneId zone)` returns the job's next run as a `ZonedDateTime` in **the zone asked for**, or an **empty** `Optional` when the legacy scheduler returns `null`.

cases.says: A job scheduled at a moment reads back at that moment.
Scheduling a second job does not move the first, although the legacy scheduler keeps the Date it was given.
A job the legacy scheduler does not know gives an empty Optional.
A run at 10:00 UTC reads back as 19:00 in Asia/Tokyo when asked for Tokyo.

concepts: java.time is used inside the application, and legacy types appear only where an old API demands them, converted at that boundary.
Date.toInstant() and Date.from(Instant) are the primary bridge between java.util.Date and java.time.
